families.s: HSE WEEE machinery, manual-handling, sharp-edge and fire-risk guidance
families.t: crushing, grinding, conveying, baling, compacting, palletising, heavy white goods, repetitive dismantling, sharp edges, electrical testing, batteries and refrigerants
f: WEEE treatment may use crushing, grinding, conveying, baling, compacting and palletising machinery.
Heavy appliances and televisions create manual-handling and stacking risks.
Repetitive removal of wiring and components can cause upper-limb disorders.
Broken equipment, sharp edges and knives can cause cuts and abrasions.
Electrical testing is required where refurbishment or reuse work is undertaken.
Refrigerators can contain hydrocarbons, ammonia and flammable insulation materials.
Removed batteries should be segregated in appropriately labelled containers to reduce fire risk.
Machinery guarding, safe stacking, handling aids and controlled dismantling should be planned as one system.
families.g: WEEE process risk depends on equipment and components, machine and dismantling method, item mass and stack, sharp and electrical hazards, refrigerants and batteries, guarding, handling aids and competence.

families.s: HSE scrap-metal unexpected-item, fire and radioactive-contamination guidance
families.t: batteries, aerosols, cylinders, flammables, public drop-off, radiation monitoring, action plans, RPA, isolation and worker training
f: Scrap-metal recycling can cause serious injury and ill health and may involve public or trader drop-off.
Scrap loads can contain unexpected batteries, aerosols, gas cylinders and flammable contamination.
Sites should screen and segregate items that could create fire, explosion or pressure hazards.
Radioactive contamination may occur in scrap consignments and can affect workers and the public.
Where contamination is foreseeable, monitoring systems should be checked and tested.
An action plan should cover characterisation, recovery, temporary storage and disposal of a discovered source.
A radiation protection adviser should support the arrangements where required.
Suspect loads should be isolated or returned under a controlled system, with workers trained to follow the procedure.
families.g: Scrap risk depends on load provenance and screening, batteries and pressure items, flammable contamination, radiation likelihood, monitoring and action plans, public access, isolation and competence.

families.s: HSE end-of-life vehicle depollution, petrol recovery and airbag-control guidance
families.t: fuel, oils, brake fluids, petrol draining, seals, supports, shock absorbers, airbags, biohazards, PPE and waste-transfer information
f: End-of-life vehicles must be depolluted by removing and controlling fuels, oils, brake fluids and other liquids.
Petrol recovery creates significant fire, explosion and skin-exposure risk.
Draining equipment should maintain an effective seal until petrol removal is complete.
Powered tool supports can reduce the need to work directly under fuel tanks.
A vehicle must be securely supported on a suitable rig before people work beneath it.
Airbag detonation creates very high noise and should be remotely controlled from suitable protection where necessary.
Vehicles contaminated with sharps or body fluids require a biohazard assessment and unsafe depollution tasks may need to be omitted.
Undeployed airbags, omitted depollution and other residual hazards should be identified in the waste-transfer information.
families.g: ELV depollution risk depends on fuel and fluid inventory, draining and support system, airbag status, contamination and sharps, tools and PPE, fire controls, waste information and competence.

families.s: HSE waste-aerosol segregation, processing and hazardous-waste guidance
families.t: domestic aerosols, full cans, commercial waste, baling, flattening, shredding, flammable contents, ignition, segregation and specialist treatment
f: Only suitable domestic-stream aerosols should normally enter mixed-waste processing at a materials-recovery facility.
Aerosols may only be baled, flattened or shredded where appropriate precautions are in place.
Full or partly full aerosol canisters in bulk should be treated as hazardous waste.
Commercial-stream aerosols should generally be directed to specialist recycling facilities.
Residual propellant and product can create fire, explosion, pressure and chemical hazards.
Incoming-waste controls should identify and segregate unsuitable aerosol loads.
Processing equipment, ventilation and ignition controls should reflect the credible release scenario.
Emergency and fire arrangements should cover damaged cans, leaks, machine jams and abnormal heating.
families.g: Waste-aerosol risk depends on source and fill state, propellant and product, quantity and segregation, processing method, machinery and ignition, ventilation, storage and emergency response.

families.s: HSE composting bioaerosol, RPE and enclosed-site atmosphere guidance
families.t: green waste, microorganisms, shredding, turning, screening, risk zones, P2/P3 RPE, vehicle cabs, leachate, biogas and public distance
f: Warm moist green waste supports rapid microorganism growth and bioaerosol generation.
Repeated high exposure can cause inhalation fever, asthma, bronchitis or allergic alveolitis.
Shredding, turning, screening and moving compost are high-exposure activities.
A COSHH assessment should identify high-emission areas, tasks and people at risk.
Routine P2 or P3 respiratory protection may be required near active processing and leachate transfer.
Enclosed vehicle cabs can provide a physical barrier if filtration and maintenance remain effective.
Enclosed buildings may accumulate carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide and vehicle exhaust, creating asphyxiation risk.
Exposure controls should also consider hygiene, dermatitis, vermin-borne infection, weather, public distance and emergency arrangements.
families.g: Composting risk depends on feedstock and biological activity, process and distance, weather and enclosure, cabs and ventilation, RPE, leachate and gas, hygiene, maintenance and worker susceptibility.
